title: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Over geological time small genera have often increased greatly in number of species, and large genera have often reached a maximum, declined and disappeared.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: geology plainly tells us that small genera have in the lapse of time often increased greatly in size; and that large genera have often come to their maxima, declined, and disappeared.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera”. Scope: genera in the fossil record

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-09: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.79

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The Paleobiology Database directly supports genus-level richness trajectories over extensive intervals. Sampling-standardization methods make the qualitative historical propositions testable despite fossil bias.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct genus richness through stratigraphic time from fossil occurrences and estimate transitions from small to large and trajectories after peak richness. Frequent large expansions of initially small genera and peak-to-extinction declines support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Genus concepts change taxonomically.

Preservation and collection effort vary through time.

fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.86
analysis feasibility: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The Paleobiology Database is built for exactly this richness-through-time question, and a standardized analysis is routine for a small team. What it can resolve well is the marine shelly subset, not genera in the fossil record as a whole. Sampling and preservation biases are serious enough that raw peaks and declines are only partly informative, even though the direction of a corrected test is clear.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From occurrence counts in time bins, reconstruct genus-richness trajectories and estimate how often small genera later become much richer and how often rich genera peak, decline, and disappear. Those two frequencies being high, after sampling standardization, would support the geological generalization; trajectories dominated by flat or monotonically biased richness would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Last occurrences are smeared backward by incomplete sampling.

Shelly marine animals dominate the usable record, so plants and terrestrial genera are a biased remainder.

Uncorrected richness rises toward the present because of rock area and preservation, independent of true diversification.
